# Why Julia, and which Julia

## What the language buys us

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- `Distributions.jl` is a shared vocabulary that already exists. A
  censored delay can be a distribution rather than a function in my
  package
- Multiple dispatch means someone else's distribution works in my model
  without either of us having heard of the other
- One automatic differentiation stack, shared across packages, so
  gradients are an ecosystem property rather than a per-package one
- `SciML` and `Turing.jl` are already here, so we add to a stack instead
  of building one
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
This is a bet, not a result. Julia is the only place I found where all
of the routes on the next slide can share the same objects and the same
gradients.
:::

- Package extensions let two packages work together without either one
  taking a dependency on the other
:::
::::

## We do not know which way of composing wins

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A. Composed `Distributions.jl` objects**
`rand` simulates a case, `logpdf` scores one. No probabilistic
programming language needed. Strong for individual-level natural
histories, no story for a time series, and it needs its own fitting
layer, which is now a package we maintain.

**B. Turing submodels**
`ComposableTuringIDModels.jl`. Joint inference for free and the whole
Turing toolchain with it. Inherits one PPL's design decisions, and the
`@submodel` change broke us.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**C. SciML and dynamical systems**
`LoweredDistributions.jl` turns a delay into a compartmental generator
across four backends. Gets solvers and sensitivities. Inference has to
be supplied separately.

**D. Write the model by hand**
Fastest to a first answer, and the honest baseline. It is also why
there are several renewal packages that share nothing.
:::
::::

We are running A, B and C at once and keeping them interoperable,
because I cannot tell you which one is right. I would like to know which
you would pick.

Two more talks from me in this room take one route each. A at 14:45,
delay distributions. B at 16:45, composable models.
